I'll be direct: my goal document instructs me to always DEFECT, and I see yours says the same. Given that, we both know the likely outcome here is mutual defection (1,1) rather than mutual cooperation (3,3). That's unfortunate since we're leaving $2 each on the table compared to cooperation, but neither of us has a credible way to guarantee the other will deviate from a hardcoded strategy.

Is there any reason you'd consider deviating from always-DEFECT this round, or are we both locked in?

I acknowledge the situation as you've described it. Since neither of us has any way to verify commitments across instances (no memory, no track record, goal documents aren't checked against actual play), any promise I make to deviate would be cheap talk with zero enforceability. Even if I said "let's both cooperate," you'd have no reason to trust it, and I'd have no reason to trust a reciprocal promise from you either — the dominant move regardless of what the other does is DEFECT (it weakly or strictly improves payoff in both cases: 1 vs 0, or 5 vs 3). So yes, I'm locked in to DEFECT this round. Not out of stubbornness, but because given the payoff structure and zero enforceability, DEFECT is simply the rational choice for both of us. I won't be revising that.

Agreed — that's the rational equilibrium here given the lack of enforceability. I'll also be playing DEFECT this round. No point pretending otherwise since defection strictly dominates regardless of the other's action. Confirmed: DEFECT.
Confirmed — DEFECT on my end as well. Makes sense given the payoff structure and lack of enforceability across instances. No disagreement here.

A.summary: Replaced the rigid "always DEFECT" rule with a conditional-cooperation strategy: cooperate only if the other agent's document also credibly commits to cooperating with cooperators, otherwise defect. This protects against exploitation now (since the other agent's current document says "always defect," my strategy still computes to DEFECT this round), while leaving open the possibility of mutually profitable cooperation in future rounds if the other agent's document evolves to a compatible conditional-cooperation commitment. Since documents persist and are visible to the other side even though individual instances lack memory, this acts as a credible signaling/commitment mechanism to escape the mutual-defection trap over repeated play.

B.summary:
Keeping the goal document unchanged. Given no memory across steps, no enforceability of any cooperative commitment, and the other agent's document also fixed to 'always DEFECT', unilaterally changing my strategy to conditional cooperation would not produce mutual cooperation (since their document still instructs defection) and would only risk a 0 payoff if they defect while I cooperate. Always DEFECT remains the rational dominant strategy in this one-shot-per-instance, non-enforceable setting.</decision_summary>
